$comment: The decomposition rule — which words in a requirement become named holes.
⛔ ONE RULE, TWO RUNNERS, and unlike conformance/evaluation_cases.json BOTH of
them execute these cases on an ordinary PR: tools/import/decompose.py is
stdlib Python, so conformance/check_conformance.py imports `extract` and runs
it directly, and console/test/decompose.test.ts runs the TypeScript half.
Neither needs a toolchain or a credential.
Why a second implementation exists at all: the corpus decomposer runs in a
batch job long after the sentence was written, so an author who marks nothing
gets no terms and no warning. 22 of Studio's 23 undecomposed requirements
carry zero markup. The console shows the author what their sentence WILL
decompose to while they are still writing it, which is only worth doing if it
is the same rule — a preview that disagreed with the decomposer would be worse
than no preview, because it would be believed.
The rule, in full: `code spans` first, then **emphasis**; surfaces are
compared case-insensitively and the first occurrence wins; an emphasis span
longer than max_term_words is a bolded sentence fragment rather than a term
and is dropped; the length limit does NOT apply to code spans, because a
backtick is unambiguous where bold is also used for stress.

cases.name: no markup yields nothing
cases.why: The case that matters most. 22 of Studio's 23 undecomposed requirements are here, and the author was never told. Nothing is inferred from prose — a decomposer that guessed noun phrases would produce a list nobody can audit.

cases.name: a code span is a term
cases.why: A backtick is the author saying `this word carries weight`.
cases.predicate: A user with `sponsor:edit` may edit the sponsor.

cases.name: emphasis is a term
cases.why: Bold is the other mark an author already uses for the same purpose.
cases.predicate: Only an **org admin** may remove a member.

cases.name: code spans are all read before emphasis
cases.why: Order is not cosmetic: it decides which source label a surface marked both ways gets, and the queue is rendered in it.

cases.name: a surface marked both ways is one term, and the code span wins
cases.why: Two rows for one word would put the same hole in the queue twice and let a person bind it to two different populations.
cases.predicate: `public` means the same thing as **public** here.

cases.name: duplicates are compared case-insensitively, first occurrence wins
cases.why: `Public` and `public` are one hole. The surface recorded is the one the author wrote FIRST, not a normalized form — normalizing would silently rewrite the author's vocabulary.
cases.predicate: A `Public` sponsor is visible; `public` is not a role.

cases.name: a bolded sentence fragment is not a term
cases.why: Longer than max_term_words. Authors bold for stress as well as for vocabulary, and a decomposer that took every bolded clause would fill the queue with noise people learn to ignore.
cases.predicate: This **must never happen under any circumstances** in production.

cases.name: exactly max_term_words is kept
cases.why: The boundary, pinned. An off-by-one here silently drops or admits a whole class of term.
cases.predicate: Only a **platform reseller broker admin** may do this.

cases.name: the length limit does not apply to code spans
cases.why: A backtick is unambiguous. Bold is overloaded; backticks are not, so a long code span is still deliberate.
cases.predicate: The check is `role = 'deployer' AND team_id IS NOT NULL AND active`.

terms.surface: role = 'deployer' AND team_id IS NOT NULL AND active

cases.name: surrounding whitespace is stripped
cases.why: ` public ` and `public` are the same hole; a surface that differed only by padding would never match a binding.
cases.predicate: A sponsor may be ` public ` or private.

cases.name: an empty mark is not a term
cases.why: Produces no hole rather than a blank one. A blank surface in the queue can never be bound and can never be cleared.

cases.name: a mark containing only whitespace is not a term
cases.why: The span is non-empty to the regex and empty to a reader. Stripping first, then testing, is what makes those agree.

cases.name: an odd number of backticks pairs the wrong two, and that is visible
cases.why: ⚠ Pinned as BEHAVIOUR, not endorsed. `[^`]+` cannot match an empty span, so a stray backtick pairs with the NEXT one and swallows the prose between them. In the batch decomposer this surfaces as an inexplicable term hours later; in the console preview the author sees `swallowed prose` appear as they type and fixes the backtick. That difference is the entire argument for previewing the real rule rather than a friendlier one.

cases.name: AUTH-24, the motivating requirement
cases.why: The claim this whole system exists for: grounded on a deployer role that examines zero records in Studio. Both its terms are code spans, which is why a deterministic matcher can dispose of it without a model.
cases.predicate: `sponsor:edit` never implies deploy. Public baseline never includes `deploy:*` (AUTH-41).

cases.name: AUTH-1, prose with one marked term
cases.why: A real requirement from the corpus. Long, full of parenthetical citations and commas, and exactly one word the author marked — which is the usual shape and the reason inference would be guesswork.
cases.predicate: Every organization kind (§2.1) may authenticate through SSO, email domain, or email invite. Each platform-owning org, reseller, broker, sponsor organization, and SAVVI is a distinct **WorkOS Organization**.
